title: Ashvamedhika
hook: a sage in the desert hears the war is over and threatens to curse Krishna for not stopping it
carry: because of who was holding the cup

segments.voice: Yesterday in Ashvamedhika, Arjuna admitted he'd forgotten the Gita, and Krishna taught again through old stories, the Anugita. Your line was I've forgotten it. Did you get one forgotten thing back? Day eight hundred sixty-nine.

Krishna is heading home to Dwaraka, crossing a desert, when he meets an old friend: the sage Uttanka, who has spent a long time in austerity and hasn't heard the news. Uttanka greets him warmly and asks, so, did you make peace between the cousins? Krishna tells him the truth. There was no peace. The Kauravas are dead. And the sage's face changes. You could have stopped it, Uttanka says, and you didn't. He raises his hand to curse the man standing in front of him. Today, what Krishna says back, and a cup of water that comes later.
screen: `A SAGE IN THE DESERT.` → `"DID YOU MAKE PEACE?"` → `HE RAISES HIS HAND TO CURSE.`

segments.voice: Krishna doesn't flinch, and he doesn't argue first. Hear me out, he says, and then decide. He tells Uttanka that he tried, that he went to the Kauravas himself, and they would not listen. Then he speaks about his own nature, and, in the epic's telling, shows Uttanka the same vast universal form Arjuna saw before the battle. The sage lowers his hand. Krishna offers him a gift, and Uttanka, who lives in this dry country, asks for something simple: water, whenever he needs it. Think of me, Krishna says, and you'll have it. Some time later, Uttanka is wandering, desperately thirsty, and he remembers. And who comes toward him? A hunter, an outcast by the rules of the time, filthy, surrounded by dogs, offering him water. Uttanka is disgusted, and refuses. He sends the man away. Then Krishna appears and explains. That was Indra, king of the gods. Krishna had asked him to bring Uttanka the drink of immortality, amrita. Indra agreed, but chose to bring it in that form, to see what the sage would do. And Uttanka turned it down because of who was holding the cup. So the angry sage who judged Krishna by the outcome of a war has just judged a gift by the look of its giver. Krishna still gives him something: clouds that will rain water for him in the desert whenever he thinks of them.
screen: `"HEAR ME OUT FIRST"` · `THE BOON: WATER IN THE DESERT` · `AN OUTCAST HUNTER OFFERS A DRINK` · then, large: `IT WAS INDRA, CARRYING AMRITA`

segments.voice: Sit, and let your breath slow. Bring to mind someone you've written off, someone whose help you'd refuse because of who they are, or how they look, or what they once did. You don't have to change your mind about them. Just breathe in and picture them holding out something you need. Breathe out and notice what rises in you. Stay with that honestly. If you pray, you can hold that person in your prayer, just as they are. The bell holds the time.
Ashvamedhika. The book where a sage refuses the drink of immortality because of who was holding the cup.
Your line: because of who was holding the cup. Today, when help comes from someone you didn't expect, take a second look before you turn it away. Day eight hundred sixty-nine.

howItsDone: Uttanka's meeting with Krishna is told in the Ashvamedhika Parva, and storytellers retell the episode of Indra's disguised gift as a lesson about judging people by appearance.

fork.setup: you're Uttanka, dying of thirst in the desert. a filthy stranger surrounded by dogs holds out water. what do you do?
options: ask him who he is first.
fork.reveal: Uttanka refuses. Krishna then tells him it was Indra, bringing him amrita.

original.note: amrita: the drink of immortality that Indra brought in disguise.

trapdoor: what you thought: Uttanka was right to be angry about the war.
what it means: he judged Krishna by the outcome before hearing him out.
what a scholar hears: the story pairs two judgments: one of Krishna by the war's end, one of a gift by the look of its giver.
